Fees from Fleur Hotels stood at Rs. 95.8 crore in FY26, an increase of 8% YoY, which is partially subdued due to the impact of GST change and accelerated renovation in the Fleur portfolio. Total management fees for Lemon Tree stood at Rs. 169.7 crore in FY26, an increase of 14% YoY. Lastly, the Indian hospitality market continues to be in favo urable structural position, demand is consistently outpacing supply in the mid -market segment , and which is where exactly we operate. Now I will hand over to Saurabh to give an update on Fleur.

Thank you, Neel endra . Thank you, everyone, for joining us on the call. I want to spend a few minutes on Fleur's business and pipeline. Post -scheme, Fleur will be India's largest hotel platform by inventory with 5,600 rooms and 39 operational hotels. While we operate pan -India , our economics are concentrated in top 6 cities that have structurally high barriers to entry and growing demand. We currently have 4 hotels with 875 rooms in our confirmed pipeline of which 572 rooms at Nehru Place, which is going to be the North India's largest hotel are under the final approval stage before we commence construction. We have finalized the design for Aurika, Nehru Place, a glimpse of which you can see in the annexure section of the investor presentation. […] Combined with Warburg Pincus primary investment commitment and strong internal accruals, we now have the capital structure and the institutional backing to expand our top line even further. We are focused on urban markets with structurally deep demand, lei sure markets, and international destinations that Indian travellers visit frequently. On the pipeline, I can tell you that we were evaluating a healthy and growing number of opportunities. We work across deal types, whether that is acquiring an asset, existing asset or development of new hotel, Fleur's peer -leading margins and in - house development capabilities are key differentiators that compress the time and risk in underwriting new opportunities. We are not very rigid on structures, but we are very disciplined on returns. There are only a few players in the market that can build hotels at th is scale and efficiency as Fleur. This is a genuine competitive advantage in the market where good assets do not always come packaged neatly. Now I hand over the forum to Pat anjali to give an update on composite scheme of demerger.

I want to take this opportunity to continue the conversation on the demerger scheme. This time with the results we have shared pro forma financials for both Lemon Tree Hotels Limited and Fleur Hotels Limited as they would appear upon the demerger scheme be coming effective. The transaction itself is very simple. Warburg has completed the purchase of APG's stake in Fleur. Next, Lemon Tree will transfer 17 hotels and development capabilities in exchange for which Lemon Tree shareholders will get Fleur shares, leading to Fleur's listing as a separate entity. This scheme will result in 2 distinct financially sound businesses. Lemon Tree Hotels as a pure -play, asset -light company focused on offering hotel management, brand loyalty distribution and digital services. Fleur Hotels will operate as a large -scale growth -oriented hotel ownership/leasing platform with end -to-end in-hous e development capabilities and potentially, as Saurabh mentioned, a very large pipeline with a significant pool of available capital. Each entity will have its own management team, capital structure and growth priorities while continuing to benefit from long -term operating agreements and arrangements and strategic alignment. Post the reorganization, Lemon Tree will emerge as a debt -free, high-margin, high ROCE company generating strong free cash flows from fees and brand -related income. Fleur Hotels will consolidate ownership of our group's existing hotels, all of which will be fully renovated by the time of the demerger. From a shareholder perspective, the scheme is designed to unlock value while preserving continuity. Post reorganization , Lemon Tree shareholders will effectively own close to 74% of Fleur Hotels, 33% directly and about 41% indirectly through Lemon Tree. This is, of course, before any primary infusion by Warburg Pincus, and this is versus the 59%, which Lemon Tree directly owns in Fleur today. Post scheme , Lemon Tree and Fleur will continue to enjoy synergistic benefits. Long - term management contracts give Lemon Tree stable and growing fee income from Fleur and Fleur can also under write new opportunities with certainty and speed with Lemon Tree as the management partner, while retaining strategic flexibility where the opportunity warrants for the other brands. Today, as Executive Chairman, I continue to chair both companies with direct ownership in each. My primary focus will be on delivering the Fleur pipeline and growth as its Executive Chair. In Lemon Tree , I will cease to hold an executive role March 2027 onwards and transition to non -Executive Chair. Our core values, including our commitment to being an employer of choice and foster ing an inclusive diverse culture will remain central to how both platforms operate as we enter this next phase of accelerated growth. With this, we come to the end of our opening remarks, and I would like to ask the moderator to open the forum for any questio ns that you may have.

I have 2 simple questions . So first, tomorrow after demerger, if Fleur believes that its inventory can be managed by some other operator and not Lemon Tree, how would that happen? Is it goes beyond arm's length basis, or can you please give a bit of colour on that?

Okay. First point, Achal, is that when Warburg came in, one of the things they did was check the quality and the economics of our management contracts and compare it to other similar operators and I think they were quite happy with the fact that we were very much in sync with that. Now the point is that if a new asset comes under development or acquisition, and it makes more sense for some other brand to operate it, then I can assure you as the F leur Chairman, that we will make sure that happens. However, having said that, there is a long relationship between Fleur and Lemon Tree and if we continue to deliver the results that we do in the mid -market segment, especially in the upscale segment, then there is also no reason why Lemon Tree will also be considered. And if the economics make sense, then Fleur will go with Lemon Tree. Short answer, brand agnostic but with one caveat that obviously Lemon Tree should not be discriminated against when opportunities arise.
But then, is not that the loss of a management fees for Lemon Tree?

Yes. But Lemon Tree must be able to deliver best results to get it . Just because Lemon Tree has skin in the game with Fleur does not mean that it has an automatic right to any asset that Fleur develops. Let me give you an example. It will I think answer your question. We bid recently for a 5 -star hotel. The economics were compelling. It was through NCLT. Unfortunately, we did not get it. It was run by another international brand and run very successfully by t hat international brand. The reason it was under NCLT , it was basically a financial structuring problem, and the owner had obviously gone bust. We did what would be a fair price for Fleur to buy it, assuming the same management contract. Unfortunately, it did not happen because we had an ultra -high net worth individual who outbid us. But my point here being that if we had bought it, we would have kept the contract with the existing operator.

That is very helpful. My second question is on Fleur. So, regarding the expansion to the 2,500 extra rooms that is supposed to be added. I just wanted to understand the thought, are we going to more Aurika, more Premier within that or is it going to be more evenly spread between Lemon Tree, Lemon Tree business a s well? And even across markets, are we looking at more metros, are we looking at non - leisure markets? Any thought process? And, if it will be going to be greenfield investments or are you also looking at expansion strategies? And what will be the timeline for that? Just a broad thought on that would be very helpful?
I will ask Saurabh, as the CEO of Fleur to answer that.

The rooms which we are talking about 2,500, they are under various stages of discussions. And we are very sure that the capital coming in from Warburg Pincus and the strength of the balance sheet as well as our entire project teams sitting on the Fleur sid e. So, it is a combination which I would say, none of the any peers have. Given that, we are confident that we will be able to add that many rooms from a strategy of investment locations, we are, like we said, around a large amount of Fleur's revenue comes from the top 6 cities in India. And this remains a core city and will invest into u pscale and upper upscale, which is between Aurika and Lemon Tree Premium and from a location perspective, we would like to be more in the top 6 cities. And from the kind of investment, we are looking at greenfield, we are looking at operating hotels, we are looking at brown fields all kind of assets. However, it must be core micro market within those 6 -7 cities and some international destinations where Indians are traveling and very selective leisure markets.

My first question was on our Fleur demerger timeline . Earlier, we had mentioned that merger will be completed 12 months in Jan. Now the slide mentions that it will take another 12 to 15 months for SEBI and other approvals. Can you just highlight the new timeline for the demerger?
The CCI approval came in April. We are still awaiting. Kapil, can you give some flavour on this? You and Mayank?

Yes. So, we are current at the stage of shareholders and the SEBI approval. That is the normal process before we file with the NCLT. There is 1 month delay only from that perspective. Generally, it takes 3 months for stock exchange. I would say 1 month delay . This estimate, which has been given a little conservative estimate because there are certain things which are procedural and especially, I would talk about the NCLT, which is a process depends on many factors . It could be shorter also; we will try our best to how fast it could be done. But looking at the procedural of first motion order, second motion, in between, there would be shareholder approval and creditors approval as well. So that is why we are taking that much time, but it does not mean that it would go into end of CY27. That is not the case. So, we would not be far away from what we said earlier.

Actually, the real issue is NCLT. Will it take 6 months? Will it take 9 months? Will it take 12 months? We have been given multiple possible timelines by experts in this. If that happens earlier, then it will be 12 months from now. If it happens later, then it will be 18 months. So, I am giving you an outer limit.

Just one small observation. Our management fee income from third party was up by about 29%, which was a very healthy growth but the same from Fleur was up by only 3%. Does it imply that the managed portfolio was relatively less insulated from the Middle Ea st crisis as compared to Fleur, or is there something more to read into this?

No. You see a large part of our fees comes from incentive fee, which is delivery of EBITDA at different slabs. Our incentive fees can go from 1% of revenue to 5% of revenue based on which slab of GOP or hotel level EBITDA we are at. Now what happened was t hat during this year, we aggressively renovated a lot of the owned portfolio, with a lot, obviously, Fleur hotels in that portfolio. GST impact and the elevated renovation impact dropped the EBITDA margins. As a result, our incentive fees were significantly affected. That is, again, linked to our delivery of EBITDA. Now if it picks up, as I am hoping it will, then obviously our fee will pick up proportionately.

Plus, Jinesh, the only other thing to add apart from what Patanjali was saying is that when you look at the management of third franchise hotels, I will give you the full year picture now. The full year fee growth was 23% in the third -party hotels and Fleur was 8%. 8% broadly because the same reason as Patanjali said, and the reason is 23% is because it is both same -store and scale revenue. There were net additions in the third -party owner, let us say, base of hotels and therefore, it is a 23% increase on a base -to-base. For Fleur hotels, the 8% full year number is based on a same - store basis, because there was no additional rooms added in that base. Making sense?

Just one question from my side. Have we set aside any total CAPEX or capital outlay, specifically for this proposed addition of 2,500 Keys across Fleur going ahead, which I believe is over the next 2 -3 years' time?

If you look at acquisitions today, depending on sellers' need and buyers' need, it is available anywhere from 8x of EBITDA to 16x of EBITDA. In some trophy assets, which we are not interested in, it could be even higher. The capital we put aside is 2. One is if we are buying an existing asset, we obviously will have to pay a higher price for it, because it is an operating asset, it has EBITDA upfront and the maximum investment we would make would be in renovation, if required, which obvio usly we adjust in our acquisition price. If we build ourselves, then it is naturally much cheaper, but there is time to market in that case. If I look at the committed capital from Warburg, this is entirely contingent upon availability of the right deals and that 2,500 active discussions are many of them right deals. If I take Fleur and Warburg's investment into account, we have the potential to deploy up to Rs. 3,000 crore in the next 12 -18 months. Now will we deploy it? If all the 2,500 come plus everything that we are doing, then yes, we will deploy it. If it does not happen, we will deploy less. That is one. Point number 2 is our current assets like Nehru Place. Nehru Place will, best guess, require Rs. 700 crore. As Saurabh had mentioned earlier, it is the single largest asset in North India. The next largest is a neighbour of ours here called Andaz, which is 525 rooms. This hotel, the cash flow will be over the next 3.5 years with 60% in the last 18 months, because that is when real money goes into finishing a hotel so we feel that we can build through our internal accruals . So the cash that we have available, which is from Warburg and our own likely free cash flow in this financial year plus debt, should safely enable us to buy these 2,500 rooms, if all fructify and any other opportunistic acquisitions which align with the strategy of core markets, high leisure demand markets or international markets where millions of Indians travel.

My first question is on margin side, like for the Lemon Tree Hotels and the Fleur Hotels, so when I look at our cost savings that we are estimating is going forward, so most of the cost saving is coming from the renovation expense coming down. All the flow through in the margins will go to Fleur Hotels. Is that understanding, correct? Sir, how much steady -state margi n in FY27 - FY28 margin, how much are we thinking for the Fleur Hotels?
Margin . Well, pre -fees, these same stores should be in the late 50s, pre -fees.
During the January call for the demerger announcement, we said that Lemon Tree Hotels' PAT margin would be around 60% .
PAT margins? No, not PAT margin. I assume you are talking EBITDA margins.
In the January call, you stated that, sir. That is why.
No, I only talk EBITDA. PAT I never talk about. I think review what I said. It would be EBITDA. Anyway, let us assume it is EBITDA. What is the question please ask?
Congratulations on a great set of numbers. My question was towards 2,500 room deals and with or without it, what sort of peak debt number are you comfortable with?

You look at our debt -to-EBITDA today, it is about 2.25 . See, in a high -growth company with stable earnings, you can technically go 4x debt -to-EBITDA. But we are, I think, much more conservative. If we deploy Rs. 1,500 crore of capital and we would probably borrow and our debt would go to mid Rs. 2,500 crore to Rs. 3,000 crore as a consolidated entity of Fleur, which means that our debt -to-EBITDA would temporarily go up till the EBITDA started flowing in. Now this is, of course, also a question of how much of these 2,500 rooms have existing EBITDA and how many will give EBITDA after a year or 2 years? It would be a mix and match. I cannot comment. It depends on which of these 2,500 rooms we finalize. I thin k this question you could perhaps ask us 12 months from now or earlier, if possible.

It was just directionally more than anything, but I will just squeeze in a quick last one, if you do not mind. For the next 5 years, again, directionally, could you give us an understanding where you foresee like CAGR growth for Lemon Tree, the platform owner, the asset -light over the next 5 years no w that you have freed up , it is a very asset -light company, it is a lot of capital deployed and so much opportunity. How do you see the next 5 years?

See, let us go back for a minute. I do not want to give guidance, but I can give you a direction. We are signing 5,000 rooms a year. I think that will accelerate. One of the key resources we have hired or Neel endra has hired, is a top line business development head who has aggressively gone with his team to go and get more hotels. Remember, 2.5 million rooms in India unbranded. We have strong strengths to convert most of them because they are in our sweet spot, which is the mid -market to upper mid -scale segment. We have grown our fees at only 23%, I am using the word only. That is with about 6,000 branded rooms under the manageme nt contract side, keep Fleur aside for a moment. If Fleur adds that 2,500 plus the 1,000 rooms under construction or 800 rooms under construction, then Fleur site will increase 60% in the next 3 years, in terms of operating assets. Those fees will come directly to Lemon Tree. Hopefully, unless there are some hotels which go to some other brand. As far as the managed portfolio goes, we are talking about maybe 2,000 rooms opening in FY27. In FY23, I do not know the number but certainly by FY another 2, 3 years from now, we will be opening 5,000 rooms a year, because that is what we are signing now. You can do the math then. You say FY27, we will open 2,000 rooms and we have 11,000 rooms. In FY28, Fleur will start contributing more. We will open maybe 3,000 rooms. In FY29, maybe we will open 4,000 rooms . One can have a range. How many rooms we open , and you have a simple number, which is the following and this is where I would be very careful about assessment. In the first 1 or 2 years of opening a hotel, normally 1 year, the income is not stable. Our fees are subdued. The minute the hotel gets stable, then our fees start kicking in on a full basis. Really, the fees can increase by 50 % - 60% on a stable hotel. One must compensate for that and say, okay, I am opening 2,000 rooms this year. Mainly I will earn Rs. 100 a room. But next year, these 2,000 rooms will give me Rs. 150 a room. Then it will be Rs. 150 going forward. Therefore, you must do this adjustment also in the fee income for the first 12 to 18 months, depending on lower fees till stability. Okay. If you look at FY23 to FY26, our fee income of the managed portfolio grew at 27% a year. I would obviously expect it to be larger, although the base has become larger, this fee income should also grow much faster. I mean, we have projections, but I am not going to share it with you.

My apologies, we just referred to the transcript. You were talking about what I said about Lemon Tree steady state that when it becomes a pure play brand and asset owner on a steady state when our EBITDA hits 75 %-80% and taxes 22 %-25%, then you are right. There is no depreciation. There is no interest. Our PAT will be 60% of the revenue. Thank you. You said something correct and I was incorrect.

Thank you, sir for the clarification. Sir, let us say, now my second follow -up question would be on that only. Now coming to the PAT margins, in our recent quarter that we have reported, our PAT margins are coming out to be 40%. For the FY25, it was 45%. How are we planning to increase those t o 60%? Because most of the margin flow-through is going to go to Fleur rather than Lemon Tree. Because of technological expenses are going to be staying at 0.7% or 0.9% of the revenue. Can you help us understand a bit more on how the margins will increase and because all the technical expense will go to Lemon Tree, if I am not wrong?

Post restructuring, Lemon Tree is expected to generate substantial free cash flow over the coming years, right? How are you thinking about capital allocation? Like would the priority be to reinvest in adjacent growth opportunities or return the excess capital to shareholders through buybacks or dividends?

Lemon Tree will not need any significant capital other than potentially investments in technology or in marketing and so on. It will be essentially a zero -debt cash accretive company. What we will do is, I think we will sit down as a Board and decide what our dividend distribution or give back to shareholder policy yet. Lemon Tree will effectively move into distribution of profit to shareholders. As far as Fleur goes, Fleur is not currently seen as a dividend distributing company, at least, currently, we would like to deploy capital because we see we can really add to shareholder value by growing the business. It will be more focused towards capit al growth or share capital growth and share value growth rather than distribution to shareholders because we think we can give a better return to shareholders simply by growing the business.

judge.what_is_spun: Agrochemicals (Crop Health Sciences) division — pesticides, insecticides, herbicides, biostimulants — demerged into Natco Crop Health Sciences Limited
judge.reason: Risk and reward of the pharmaceutical and agrochemicals verticals differ; segregation enables focused growth, operational efficiency, independent capital allocation, different investor sets, and is expected to unlock the value of the business verticals.
judge.insiders: Promoter and Promoter Group hold 8,84,65,126 of 17,91,09,870 shares (~49%); 1:1 entitlement carries that stake into the Resulting Company. Demerged Company retains 20% post-listing; director P.S.R.K. Prasad sits on Natco Crop Health Sciences' board.
judge.hidden_value: Demerged turnover was only ₹60.62 crore, 1.48% of total; FY25 agro segment result was a ₹1,458 million loss. Management says it reached ~₹140 crore sales and roughly EBITDA breakeven. Separation removes a loss-maker from pharma and exposes an early-growth agro business.
judge.selling_pressure_why: Tiny (1.48% of turnover), loss-making, different industry; 4,22,879 pharma shareholders receive 1:1 agrochemical shares, with parent holding 20%.
judge.listing_timeline: Not stated as a listing date. Board (March 24, 2026): Appointed Date 1st October 2026 and "Subsequent to the Scheme coming into effect, the Resulting Company /Transferee Company shall apply for the listing of its equity shares over Stock Exchanges in accordance with the Scheme." On the Feb 12, 2026 call management said "roughly, we're thinking by October, November" and "we should be able to do it in the next 8, 9 months"; on Nov 14, 2025 "we are targeting that for the year 2026." On September 9, 2026 the Company said it "has not filed the Scheme and related applications with the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal" and will file a revised Scheme after the Rights Issue.
judge.read_next: The revised Scheme to be filed with Stock Exchanges post Rights Issue — check the share swap ratio and agro segment numbers.
judge.quote: The segregation is also expected to unlock the value of the business verticals of the Demerged Company.

rationale.rationale: NATCO is demerging its Crop Health Sciences (Agrochemicals) division into Natco Crop Health Sciences Limited, leaving the listed parent as a pure pharmaceutical company (FDFs, APIs, oncology-led branded/complex generics). Management's stated reason is that the two verticals carry different risk-reward profiles and serve entirely different customers — Rajesh Chebiyam said the demerger "gives a more focused approach because the business, ultimately, the customers are quite different" — so a dedicated management, channel and product strategy (differentiated, patent-controlled, limited-competition molecules like the fungicide GLANZ and CTPR combinations) can be run without competing for attention inside a much larger pharma P&L. The second reason is valuation and capital: agro turnover was only INR 60.62 crore in FY25, i.e. 1.48% of total turnover, against FY25 group revenue of INR 4,784 crore and PAT of INR 1,883.4 crore, and Rajeev Nannapaneni said shareholders "will get another business which is not being valued in our system because it is of a very tiny business and a very large business in pharma"; separately listed, "it can raise its own capital and grow by itself." The timing was deliberately set after the division approached breakeven — segment loss of about INR 150 crore in FY25 (including a INR 50 crore non-cash PP&E impairment taken in Q4 FY25), narrowing to a INR 3.2 crore loss in Q1 FY26 on INR 34.7 crore of sales, EBITDA-positive at INR 52.4 crore of sales in Q2 FY26, and roughly INR 140 crore of FY26 sales versus INR 60 crore the prior year, against the INR 150–170 crore management had said was needed for EBITDA breakeven. The Scheme adds the corporate-finance logic: focused growth, operational rationalisation, optimum use of resources, and the ability for each business to "address independent business opportunities, pursue efficient capital allocation and attract different sets of investors, strategic partners, lenders and other stakeholders," plus unlocking the value of the verticals. Shareholders get 1 share of the resulting company for every 1 NATCO share, with NATCO retaining 20% of the post-listing equity to keep supporting a business "still at its early growth stages" — so holders retain 100% of the ultimate economic interest (80% direct, 20% through NATCO). The push came from public-market shareholders, not lenders or partners: an investor on the Nov 14, 2025 call asked directly about "value unlocking for the shareholders," and management separately cited shareholder feedback that NATCO's profit base was too concentrated. Agro is almost entirely domestic ("predominantly domestic" sales, with 25–30% input cost inflation flagged in 2026), which management contrasts with the export-weighted pharma business.
rationale.evolution: On the Feb 13, 2025 and May 29, 2025 calls there was no demerger talk — only agro losses, the INR 50 crore impairment and a INR 120–170 crore breakeven target; the Aug 13, 2025 call reported the loss down to INR 3.2 crore with still no mention. The board gave in-principle approval to evaluate the demerger on Sep 25, 2025, and Rajeev first discussed it publicly on the Nov 14, 2025 call ("demerge this business from the main company and list it separately... targeting that for the year 2026"), framing it as value unlocking plus the ability to raise its own capital; the board approved incorporating the wholly-owned resulting company on Nov 14, 2025. On Feb 12, 2026 the timeline was guided to "October, November" 2026 (8–9 months), and the Scheme itself was approved on Mar 24, 2026 with a 1:1 share entitlement, appointed date Oct 1, 2026 and 20% retained by NATCO; the May 29, 2026 call reiterated focus and different customers as the primary reason. By Sep 9, 2026 the Scheme had stock-exchange observation letters but had not been filed with the NCLT, because the INR 1,279.36 crore rights issue at INR 750/share (allotted Oct 23, 2026) changes the capital structure — the board decided to re-cut and re-file the Scheme after the rights issue while keeping the same swap ratio.

points.point: First public confirmation of the plan: demerge Crop Health Sciences out of the parent and list it separately, targeted for 2026, disclosed alongside the division reaching roughly EBITDA breakeven at INR 52.4 crore of quarterly sales.
points.quote: I think we have announced earlier that we will demerge this business from the main company and list it separately and we are targeting that for the year 2026.

points.point: Rajeev defines the value-unlock logic in response to an investor question: separate listing gives the business special focus and the ability to raise its own capital and grow independently, now that it is breaking even.
points.quote: Value unlocking means I think what we see is this business now is about breaking even now. So, we will list it separately and then we will have special focus on this and it can raise its own capital and grow by itself.

points.point: The core valuation argument: the agro business is too small to be valued inside a pharma company of NATCO's size, and shareholders will get a complete see-through into both businesses.
points.quote: I think you will get another business which is not being valued in our system because it is of a very tiny business and a very large business in pharma.

points.point: Timeline guidance: the process has started, with an internal goal of completing in the next 8–9 months (around October–November 2026), but no firm date committed.
points.quote: I think we have started the process. So , I think roughly, we're thinking by October, November, but I don't want to say any definite time lines, but this is our, what should I say, goal to do.

points.point: Management's clearest operating rationale, from the head of Crop Health Sciences: a focused approach is needed because the agro customer base is entirely different from pharma, with FY26 agro sales of about INR 140 crore versus INR 60 crore the year before.
points.quote: So, as you're aware, so we're in the process of demerging the business. And one of the primary reasons we felt also it gives a more focused approach because the business, ultimately, the customers are quite different.

points.point: Growth plans — new differentiated, patent-controlled, limited-competition products, more channel partners and more people — are tied directly back to the demerger as the reason for sharper focus.
points.quote: So I think we're fairly confident going forward. And that's also one of the main reasons for demerging and having more focus on the business.

points.point: The Mar 24, 2026 Scheme of Arrangement grounds the demerger in differing risk-reward profiles of the pharmaceutical and agrochemicals verticals; agro turnover was INR 60.62 crore in FY25, 1.48% of total company turnover.
points.quote: The Board of Directors of the Demerged Company believe that the risk and reward associated with each of the aforesaid business verticals are different.

points.point: The Scheme's capital-markets rationale: each business can chase its own opportunities, allocate capital efficiently and attract its own investor and lender base, alongside focused growth, operational rationalisation and value unlocking.
points.quote: Each business would be able to address independent business opportunities, pursue efficient capital allocation and attract different sets of investors, strategic partners, lenders and other stakeholders.

points.point: NATCO keeps 20% of the post-listing equity of the resulting company so it can keep funding and strategically supporting an early-stage business; shareholders get 1 new share for every 1 NATCO share, retaining 100% of the ultimate economic interest (80% direct plus 20% indirect).
points.quote: Further, the Demerged Company intends to retain the current shareholding in the Resulting Company (20% of post listing shareholding) in order to continue to offer support to the Agrochemicals Business which is still at its early growth stages and help in monitoring the progress and providing strategic support.

points.point: The Nov 14, 2025 board filing states the purpose as unlocking value in the core pharmaceutical business while giving each entity operational flexibility, dedicated management and separate brand positioning.
points.quote: To demerge the Agro business of the Company into a separate entity, the move shall enable value unlocking of the core business (pharmaceuticals) and enhance long -term growth.

points.point: Pre-demerger baseline for why the division was a drag: a INR 50 crore non-cash impairment on agro property, plant and machinery in Q4 FY25, FY25 agro revenue of about INR 60 crore, and INR 160–170 crore needed just to be EBITDA positive.
points.quote: So, I think this year, we feel we are going to hit that critical mass where we'll start breaking even. We are doing about INR60 crores net revenue last year. So, I think we need to hit about INR160 crores to INR170 crores at least to have that EBITDA positive.

points.point: The Sep 9, 2026 board update: the Scheme had received observation letters from both exchanges but was not filed with the NCLT because the INR 1,300 crore rights issue changes the capital structure, so the Scheme will be amended and re-filed post-issue with the swap ratio unchanged.
points.quote: The fund raising by way of a Rights Issue proposed at the meeting of the board of directors held on September 09, 2026 is expected to result in change to the Company's capital structure and shareholding pattern and consequently would require necessary changes to the Scheme.

rationale.what_management_expects: Agro: dedicated management focus, its own capital raising, differentiated limited-competition products, growth past breakeven from roughly INR 140 crore sales. Pharma: a cleaner, focused oncology/complex-generics entity. For shareholders: value unlocked in a business "not being valued in our system," a complete see-through into both, operational efficiency, efficient capital allocation, and distinct investor/lender bases.
rationale.gaps: No standalone agro financials, debt/asset split, valuation or swap-ratio basis; no post-demerger profitability, capital needs, board/management, listing date, or revised Scheme terms.

rationale.rationale: Management presented the separation as the heart of "Vedanta 2.0": dismantling one diversified holding company into five sector-specific pure-play entities — Vedanta Aluminium Metal Ltd, Vedanta Power (renamed from Talwandi Sabo Power), Vedanta Oil & Gas (renamed from Malco Energy), Vedanta Iron & Steel Ltd, and a residual Vedanta Limited holding Zinc India (60.71% of HZL), Zinc International, Copper (Silvassa/Fujairah/KSA), FACOR ferrochrome and nickel/semiconductor assets — on the stated logic that each would "chart out their own growth trajectory and attract respective thematic investors," with sharper accountability and separate dividend policies set by five independent boards. The first problem they said it solves is valuation: one monolithic entity buried the parts, and after listing on 15 June 2026 the company itself claimed the combined value of VEDL plus the four new shares went from ₹225.50 at announcement (29 Sep 2023) to ₹932.05, ">300% upside". The second is capital structure: the ~$5.5bn group net debt (earlier quoted as $6.7bn) was re-architected "aligning debt with earning strength and growth stage of each resulting company" — ~$3.5bn to Aluminium (1.3x EBITDA), Power at 4.7x but on long-dated 7–10 year PFC/REC paper, residual Vedanta Ltd ~$1bn at 0.4x, and Oil & Gas nil / Iron & Steel ≤$0.2bn net debt — against group leverage of 0.95x. Third, it removed rigid cash rules: the prescriptive policy requiring at least 30% of profit as dividend and upstreaming of Hindustan Zinc dividends within six months became "principle-based," giving each board flexibility. Fourth, it repriced intra-group charges: copper's brand fee falls from 3% to 0.75% (~$65mn on $3.1–3.2bn revenue, +2.25% EBITDA), which management expects to lift that near-trading business from ~1% to at least 5% margin in FY27, while the blended group brand fee stays ~$400–450mn and the 3% rate stands to FY29. Fifth, it opens dedicated capital pools — "differentiated capital structure" means "many anchor investors domestically and globally are very keen to come in the cap table," an extra deleveraging avenue for Vedanta Resources' remaining ~$4.7bn debt serviced out of ~$400mn brand fee plus 4–5% dividend. Third parties shaped it: lenders made debt allocation "a precondition for granting NOC"; the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas objected at NCLT over disputed Cairn arbitration dues (~$512mn) and was satisfied only by a Vedanta corporate guarantee ring-fencing the demerged oil & gas entity; and a ₹660 crore full-and-final SEPCO settlement was booked as an exceptional item "paving the way for a proposed demerger process." A second, separate demerger followed on 30 July 2026: ~2,264 acres and ~53,185 sq ft across 22 non-core real estate assets (FY26 turnover ₹1.26 crore, 0.001% of standalone revenue) go to Vedanta Property Platforms Ltd at 1 share per 20 VEDL shares, because the portfolio sat "embedded within the operating business" with "sub-optimal visibility" and a claimed ₹30,000 crore+ of latent value.
rationale.evolution: By the Feb 2025 (Q3FY25) call the scheme was already in execution with shareholder/creditor meetings set for 18 Feb 2025, and in Apr 2025 (Q4FY25) new Group CEO Deshnee Naidoo folded it into "Vedanta 2.0" with completion guided for September 2025. It then slipped repeatedly through regulatory friction: Aug 2025 (Q1FY26) disclosed the NCLT second-motion part-hearing of 2 July with the next date 20 August, an NCLAT interim stay on the TSPL power order (₹1,248 crore bank guarantee posted) and MoPNG objections; Nov 2025 (Q2FY26) set final hearing for 12 November, settled SEPCO for ₹660 crore and gave MoPNG a Vedanta corporate guarantee; Jan 2026 (Q3FY26) reported NCLT approval on 16 Dec 2025 for four businesses and 9 Jan 2026 for power, Ind AS 105 discontinued-operations accounting, and a 1 April effective-date target. Apr 2026 (Q4FY26) was the final pre-demerger call: effective and record date 1 May 2026, one VEDL share earning four additional shares, listing by mid-June, plus newly disclosed mechanics — the copper brand-fee cut, the principle-based dividend policy and holdco-level M&A. After listing, the 30 July 2026 board meeting opened a further leg by approving the real-estate demerger into VPPL, targeted for completion in FY28.

points.point: Ajay Goel positioned the demerger purely as value unlock while it was at the shareholder/creditor-approval stage, with the meeting scheduled for 18 February 2025.
points.quote: This transformative step is poised to unlock significant value for our investors.

points.point: Naidoo, in her first call as Group CEO, tied the demerger to the "Vedanta 2.0" ambition of a $100 billion critical minerals, energy and technology powerhouse, with completion then guided for September 2025.
points.quote: We are making good progress with our demerger plan, aiming to create pure-play entities that will enhance strategic focus and operational flexibility.

points.point: An investor (Ashish Kejriwal) flagged that mining leases for the Sijimali bauxite and coal blocks had to be transferred to Vedanta Aluminium before the split could close; management confirmed a parallel approvals plan.
points.quote: But the team has a detailed approvals plan, including all of the mining licenses that will start being approved, in fact, have already started the process.

points.point: Delays were attributed to two external forums — the NCLT second-motion hearing and an NCLAT stay on the TSPL power order — yet the split was named a top corporate priority.
points.quote: The execution of the demerger remains a top priority for Vedanta.

points.point: The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, a key counterparty in the oil and gas business, objected at NCLT that the demerged Cairn entity might not be able to pay disputed arbitration dues.
points.quote: And in the last NCLT hearing, they did express concern about the payments of any of the disputed dues that may become payable by Cairn in case the ongoing arbitration ruling, as we have all learned now, comes in their favor.

points.point: A long-standing creditor dispute was bought out with a ₹660 crore exceptional charge explicitly to clear the demerger path; MoPNG's objection was neutralised by a Vedanta corporate guarantee covering the full extent of the alleged claims (~$520mn).
points.quote: As part of demerger proceedings, a full and final settlement of Rs. 660 Cr has been done with SEPCO, thereby resolving a long-standing dispute, paving the way for a proposed demerger process.

points.point: Goel framed the end state as five separately valued verticals and listed all five demerged entities for the end of FY26, ahead of the final NCLT hearing on 12 November.
points.quote: On the demerger, we are at the final stage. We remain confident of completing our demerger by end of this fiscal, unlocking focused value across our five verticals.

points.point: With NCLT approval in hand (16 Dec 2025 for four businesses, 9 Jan 2026 for power), Naidoo gave the fullest statement of purpose — strategy focus, balance-sheet strength and growth — and targeted 1 April as effective date.
points.quote: This marks a defining moment in our journey, one that empowers our businesses to sharpen the strategies, strengthen the balance sheets and accelerate growth with the aim of unlocking shareholder value.

points.point: Lenders were an active party: debt allocation across entities had to be agreed with bankers before they would release no-objection certificates, with the $6.7bn consolidated net debt apportioned by assets and each entity's debt-servicing capability.
points.quote: When we went to the banker seeking NOC, in that case, debt allocation was broadly aligned with the bankers as a precondition for granting NOC for demerger approval.

points.point: Goel also framed the restructuring as a tax and structuring opportunity (accumulated losses, unabsorbed depreciation) and said it would be used to make oil and gas and iron and steel debt-free, part-funded by a 1.1% HZL OFS worth ~₹3,000 crore.
points.quote: One thing I can confirm to the entire audience and to the stakeholders at large, that demerger in fact, becomes an opportunity across the areas.

points.point: The power CEO used the demerger to justify a standalone growth mandate: from 4.2 GW today to ~4.8 GW by H1FY27 and a plan for an additional 10–12 GW over five to seven years.
points.quote: And as we demerge, we really want to be a growth company and ride the India's growth story on energy.

points.point: On the final pre-demerger call Goel set out the structural logic: five pure-plays, each attracting its own investor base, effective 1 May 2026 with one VEDL share earning four additional shares and trading expected by mid-June.
points.quote: This will entail creation of five independent sector-specific pure-play companies, allowing each company to chart out their own growth trajectory and attract respective thematic investors.

points.point: Capital structure was deliberately engineered per entity — Oil & Gas nil debt, Iron & Steel ≤$0.2bn, Aluminium ~$3.5bn at 1.3x, Power 4.7x on 7–10 year PFC/REC maturities, Vedanta Ltd ~$1bn at 0.4x — against group leverage of 0.95x.
points.quote: The de-merger has been architected with precision on capital structure, aligning debt with earning strength and growth stage of each resulting company.

points.point: The split removed prescriptive cash rules: the mandatory 30% profit payout and the six-month Hindustan Zinc dividend upstreaming requirement give way to board discretion at each of the five companies.
points.quote: Currently, Vedanta's policy on dividend is more prescriptive; it will become more descriptive.

points.point: Unbundling also repriced the brand fee for the thin-margin copper business, which management expects to lift copper margins from ~1% to at least 5% in FY27 (~$65mn benefit), while blended group brand fee stays flat and the 3% rate holds to FY29.
points.quote: So the brand fee for copper from the current 3% will go down to 0.75% and that alone from India's viewpoint means higher EBITDA by 2.25%.

points.point: Separate cap tables were pitched as a new deleveraging channel for Vedanta Resources, which still carries $4.7bn of debt against ~$400mn brand fee plus a 4–5% dividend.
points.quote: Now as we de-merge all the five companies, additionally we'll have the optionality of a differentiated capital structure and in that case, many anchor investors domestically and globally are very keen to come in the cap table, and that will be additional avenue for de-leveraging.

points.point: Asked whether the entities could still acquire outside their sector, Naidoo said business CEOs are mandated to grow organically on their own 2x/3x plans while cross-sector M&A sits at a holdco with its own team and the Chairman.
points.quote: Holdco will be set up to make sure there is some visibility of capital allocation across all 5 businesses, but also with its own M&A team to start looking at some of these opportunities.

points.point: The 30 July 2026 real-estate scheme (VEDL into Vedanta Property Platforms Ltd, 1 share for every 20) rests on the claim that ~2,264 acres and ~53,185 sq ft across 22 assets were trapped inside the operating business — FY26 turnover of just ₹1.26 crore, 0.001% of standalone revenue — with a claimed ₹30,000 crore+ of latent value.
points.quote: The real estate business is currently embedded within the operating business and the real estate portfolio has been historically subject to limited focused utilisation, resulting in sub-optimal visibility of the real estate business segment and value realization.

points.point: The stated benefits mirror the five-way split — dedicated management and governance, sector-specific investors, lenders and strategic partners, and separate financial disclosure enabling clearer valuation; VPPL may also absorb real estate from Meenakshi Energy and Incab Industries.
points.quote: enabling focused and sharper capital market access and thereby unlocking the value of the Demerged Undertaking and creating enhanced value for shareholders.

rationale.what_management_expects: Each pure-play sets its own strategy, dividend policy and capital structure: Aluminium 1.3x levered on strong cash flow, Power a 10–12 GW growth story, Oil & Gas and Iron & Steel debt-free, residual Vedanta Ltd 0.4x with HZL dividends optional and copper margins rising 1%-to-5% on a 0.75% brand fee. Thematic investors and anchor capital per cap table; simpler structures, sharper accountability, value unlock (claimed >300%).
rationale.gaps: No explanation of why these five groupings, no SOTP targets, separation costs, dis-synergies, duplicated corporate overhead, or who originally proposed the split.

Per the 15 May 2026 Regulation 30A disclosure: Twin Star Holdings Ltd "holding 40.02% shares in Vedanta Limited", Vedanta Holdings Mauritius II Limited "holding 12.60% shares in Vedanta Limited", Welter Trading Limited "holding 0.98% shares in Vedanta Limited"; Vedanta Resources Limited is "classified as a member of the promoter group of Vedanta Limited, with no direct shareholding in Vedanta Limited". At the 18 February 2025 court-convened meeting the Promoter and Promoter Group held 2,204,867,749 of 3,910,388,057 shares (record date 11 February 2025).
deal.promoter_holding_after: 2023/2026 composite demerger: "Post demerger, every Vedanta shareholder - both retail and institutional - will receive one new share in each of the newly demerged companies. Other than this, there will be no change in the overall shareholding structure." And: "The shareholders will continue to enjoy value unlocking of the Vedanta Base Metals business as part of legacy residual Vedanta where they will remain shareholders in addition to receiving equivalent shares in other resulting companies which will mirror Vedanta shareholding." 2026 real estate demerger: not stated.
deal.public_shareholders_get: 2023/2026 composite demerger: "In accordance with provisions of the Scheme, Resulting Companies issued and allotted 1 (One) fully paid-up equity share of each Resulting Companies for every 1 (One) fully paid-up equity share held in the Company, to the shareholders of the Company whose names are recorded in the register of members and / or records of the depository as on the Record Date (i.e., May 01, 2026)." Also: "Shareholders of Vedanta Limited will receive equity shares in each of the four resulting listed entities (in addition to their shareholding in Vedanta Limited) in proportion to their existing holdings, ensuring continuity of ownership while enabling direct participation in the growth trajectories of individual businesses." And: "Shareholders holding one share of Vedanta as on 29th April, today, will receive four additional shares of the resulting companies." 2026 real estate demerger: not stated (consideration is a "Share Entitlement Ratio" defined in the Scheme, value not disclosed).
deal.management_incentives: not stated
deal.insider_actions: Promoter group borrowing secured on Vedanta Limited shares: Vedanta Resources Limited (borrower) with Twin Star Holdings Ltd, Vedanta Holdings Mauritius II Limited and Welter Trading Limited as guarantors entered a facility agreement dated 30 January 2026, amended and restated on 13 May 2026 and upsized "from up to US$ 350,000,000 to US$ 600,000,000"; "Encumbrances have been created over the shares of Vedanta Limited, in terms of the Amended Facility Agreement and related finance documents, and such encumbrance(s) have been disclosed in the form and manner specified under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011", with disclosures made under Regulations 29(1) and 31 of the Takeover Regulations. Company-level selling around the separation: on 18 June 2025 Vedanta sold 66.7 million Hindustan Zinc shares (c. 1.6%) for c. INR 3,028 Cr — "As we actively progress towards the demerger of Vedanta into sector focused entities across diverse verticals, this capital raise will help de-leverage the balance sheet and enhance financial flexibility"; a further Zinc India offer-for-sale was launched on 27 January 2026 (about 1.1%, c. Rs.3,000 crore) with "the entire amount will be used for de-leveraging", taking the holding to around 60.7% from 61.8%. Also disclosed: "As part of demerger proceedings, a full and final settlement of Rs. 660 Cr has been done with SEPCO"; and a corporate guarantee from Vedanta covering the MoPNG/DGH alleged claims so they do not sit on the demerged oil and gas entity.

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Vedanta Limited (remaining) keeps about $1 billion of net debt at 0.4x net debt/EBITDA, serviceable "through FACOR, through Zinc International, and the Copper" plus Zinc India dividends; Q1FY27 net debt ₹8,299 crore and net debt/EBITDA 0.30x, gross debt ₹28,291 crore
other_differences.separated_business: Of $5.5 billion group net debt, Vedanta Aluminium takes $3.5 billion (1.3x); Vedanta Power's leverage 4.7x with mostly long-term PFC/REC debt of 7 to 10 years; Vedanta Oil and Gas debt-free; Vedanta Iron and Steel no more than $0.2 billion
other_differences.quote: So out of 5.5, 3.5 goes to Vedanta Aluminum, and looking at the EBITDA of that business, their leverage will be still 1.3.

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Continuing operations carried ₹10,522 crore of net debt as on 31 March 2026, reduced to ₹8,299 crore by 30 June 2026
other_differences.separated_business: ₹42,732 crore of the ₹53,254 crore group net debt as on 31 March 2026 went out with the discontinued (demerged) operations
other_differences.quote: At Vedanta group level pre-de-merger, our leverage stands at 0.95x, reflecting resilient EBITDA and disciplined financial structuring.

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: Q1FY27 EBITDA ₹8,469 crore on revenue ₹23,456 crore, EBITDA margin 57% (excludes copper business), up 985 bps YoY
other_differences.separated_business: Pre-demerger combined group: Q4FY26 EBITDA margin ~44% (record) and FY26 ~39%; Aluminium FY26 margin 38%, Zinc India 56%, Cairn Oil and Gas ~44%
other_differences.quote: EBITDA margin# of 57%, up by 985 bps YoY and 225 bps QoQ

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: ROCE c.29% in Q1FY27 ("ROCE is EBIT net of tax outflow divided by average capital employed")
other_differences.separated_business: Pre-demerger combined group: "Record Return on Capital Employed at ~32%, improved by 539 bps YoY" in Q4FY26; 27% in Q3FY26 and ~26% in Q2FY26
other_differences.quote: Strong Return on Capital Employed at 29%, reflecting disciplined capital allocation

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: growth capex ₹1,148 crore in Q1FY27 (project capex ₹1,181 crore and sustaining capex ₹1,390 crore in the net debt walk)
other_differences.separated_business: Pre-demerger combined group: "Total capital expenditure in the year stood at ₹ 14,918 crores" in FY26 (c.$1.7 billion), deployed across aluminium, zinc, oil and gas and power; Saudi rod mill and Gamsberg Phase 3 plans of $2 billion and $4 billion discussed for the separated/retained international businesses
other_differences.quote: Invested Growth Capex of ₹1,148 crore in Q1 FY27

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: cash and cash equivalents ₹19,992 crore at 30 June 2026 (Zinc India ₹12,892 crore of it), FCF pre-capex ₹4,412 crore in Q1FY27
other_differences.separated_business: Pre-demerger combined group: "Cash and Cash Equivalent stood at ₹28,485, improving by 38% YoY on the back of Free cash flow (pre-capex) of ₹ 26,013 crore" in FY26
other_differences.quote: Cash and cash equivalents position remains strong at ₹ 19,992 crore .

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: Q1FY27 PAT ₹5,294 crore, up 152% YoY, on continuing operations; credit rating upgraded to AA+/Stable by both ICRA and CRISIL (highest since 2014)
other_differences.separated_business: Market value created by the separated entities after listing: combined market capitalisation of the resulting companies up over ₹71,000 crore in Q1FY27
other_differences.quote: Vedanta’s demerger is unlocking significant shareholder value, with combined market cap of resulting companies growing by over ₹71,000 crore in the 1st quarter .

other_differences.parent_or_remaining: Remaining Vedanta Limited: normalized effective tax rate 26% in Q1FY27 versus 28% in Q1FY26, with a tax charge of ₹1,895 crore

other_differences.quote: Normalized ETR is 26% vs 28% in Q1’ FY26, lower due to reduced losses in subsidiaries wherein DTA is not recognized .

turns: Thank you all for joining the call today. The second quarter was defining in terms of strategic direction for Vedanta and its subsidiaries. Vedanta's Board approved the proposal to demerge the business into six independent listed entities, each one capable of executing its individual business strategies. The decision is a significant step forward in its journey of sustainable growth and greater shareholder value. The demerger would create six incredibly competitive, nimble and focused enterprises. We have filed the scheme of demerger with the stock exchang e in October 2023 and are working on next steps as we speak. We exited the second quarter with strong financial results. We delivered the highest ever second quarter consolidated revenue of INR38,546 crores, up 16% quarter -on-quarter. We have also delivered highest ever second quarter EBITDA of INR11,834 crores, up 70% quarter -on-quarter and a strong margin of 35% and PAT before exceptional items of INR4,403 crores, up approximately 3x quarter -on-quarter. Vedanta Limited November 04, 2023

Thank you, Arun, and good evening, everyone. I'm very happy to come back to Vedanta. Such a critical time as we embark on our journey of demerger and unlock significant value for shareholders. At the same time, we also reorient ourselves towards next phase of organic growth. During second quarter, the commodity prices remain under pressure, mainly due to out -shipping of supply as compared to demand growth. The global economy has slowed down, compared to last year with growing regional divergences.

Public (C4) Moving on to next page on balance sheet and debt. Net debt as on September 30 th, stands at INR57,771 crores as against INR59,192 crores as on last quarter. The net debt decreased overall majorly due to strong cash from operations and partly offset by working capital build -up and allocation of funds towards capex and returning money t o our shareholders. Our leverage ratio, which is net debt to EBITDA, stood at 1.64x, compared to 1.88x in the previous quarter. We finished the quarter with healthy cash and cash equivalents of INR1 6,702 crores. Our average maturity of debt is maintained at about three years with average cost of borrowings at about 9%. This quarter, we also transitioned to new tax regime for Vedanta Limited, a simpler tax structure starting FY '23, which is the last year. Adoption of new tax regime has resulted in onetime net MAT write -off of INR6,128 crores, but we had a net cash tax savings of INR2,040 crores for fiscal y ear 2022 and 23 from the same. The cash tax in future years will also be lower under new regime. The scheme allows companies to lower tax outgo and redeploy the same on operations, growth and shareholder value creation. A quick word on demerger. We have filed the scheme of demerger with the stock exchanges in October '23, and we are progressing well on our plan. Finally, in conclusion, the risk to the outlook are now far more balanced than they were six months ago, with the operating environment stabilizing. We remain committed to the cost and production guidance at the beginning of fiscal year 2024 and we're maki ng good progress towards our long -term goals of vertical integration, operational excellence and deleveraging. With this, I now hand over to operator for Q&A. Thank you.

Okay. The second question is on ferrochrome. Now here, our capacity expansion plans are quite, I would say, aggressive by 300 ktpa and ferrochrome, as we all know, is a power guzzler. And our larger goal is to reduce the emission. So how do we tie the powe r -- our goal of reducing emissions and enhancing ferrochrome capacity? That is one. And secondly, where do we expect to ship this ferrochrome? I mean as far as I understand, ferrochrome capacity is -- I mean, there is like, the market is quite balanced today. So why is the sudden plan of expanding in this ferrochrome? Or whether we want t o expand in stainless steel at a later stage as well?

So as is the nature the way our group operates, we have always been in business where we are the number one, number two or number three. We would not like to become a small player in a big market and continue in that status. So our ambitions are always to be in the number one, number two and ferrochrome expansion plan is no exception. That is to begin with our intention on a visionary level. Vedanta Limited November 04, 2023

Public (C4) Second, when we talk of ferrochrome, it's a key ingredient for stainless steel making. And in Indian steel production growth, if you see last 10 years, which have mostly been in the auto sectors or on the building sector, which are lon g products that peopl e have expanded. We firmly believe as GDP per capita grows, as the country grows, you will see expansion in consumption of aluminium, expansion in consumption of stainless steel. And it's not only India, entire Southeast Asia, this is going to be the situation in next five years to 10 years. And keeping that strong growth in mind, we feel that Vedanta will play a key role in that development part of India and hence the nature of th is expansion. As far as your question on ferrochrome production being power guzzler and it's been dependent on thermal pool, we need to appreciate that our own group company, Serentica is already putting up thousands of megawatts capacity of hybrid power of solar, wind, followed up by -- backup by pump hydro storage. Almost all Vedanta units are signing up with them for power supply. So most of the power supply currently signed up would land anywhere between 2024 to 2026. And I'm sure ferrochrome projects will take another three years to come up. And by that time, we will have round -the-clock renewable power agreements and the lines be ing drawn or the capacities being put up. So there would be time that we will stick to our emission reduction targets that we have set for ourselves by 2050, net zero and as well as looking at the numbers of 2040, 2030 internal targets are there. We have got our actions completely lined up as far as emissions are concerned.
So, what you're confirming is that ferrochrome plant would be fed from round -the-clock renewable power capacity?
Okay, sir. Thank you and all the best.

Sure, sir. Sir, finally, if I can just, on the aluminium CoP, we have been seeing reductions. So can we expect a further reduction in 3Q, a significant reduction apart from coal and other input costs?

If you see quarter -on-quarter . They have a steady decrease in CoP. And that trend will continue as long as their own Jamkhani productions, own coal productions have gone up and new coal mines, which is Radhikapur and Kurloi as they come into operations, we can only expect and Lanjigarh capacity expanding bauxite mine coming into play. We have a clear road map to reducing to immediate terms about $1,800 per ton and in future maybe another $200 or so, we should be able to reduce.
Sure, sir. Thank you so much.

Public (C4) Imtiaz: Thank you. Thank you for the opportunity and congrats on the second quarter performance. And Mr. Goel, great to have you back. I have two questions. The first one, can you just let us know where you are now in your attempts to sell your steel and iron ore mines?

Look, so we had -- to let the world know that we have a strategic interest in looking for strategic investors in our steel and iron ore mine business. But we are, at the same time, investing in growing the business. We are investing in debottlenecking the operations. We are investing in getting the best people to run the shops there. So these two are t wo independent activities. As of now, I won't be able to put a finger on when and to whom the final decision will go to. As and when it happens, we will let it be known.
Okay. The second question is with regards to your dividends. You received a dividend from Hindustan Zinc back in July. Any plans to pay that dividend out?

See if you look at our allocation of capital policy, Imtiaz, on the website, which is sometimes in 8th Feb, 2022, the time frame that we have committed for pass on is six months. In that case, July, we have time until January. Now you also appreciate that any dividend declaration is a board matter, and it will be, I think, a tad, I think, early in terms of comme nting what is the plan now. Overall, if you see Vedanta's current year dividend, which is about INR39 per share is far higher than what Vedanta got from the Zinc as well. So from taxation viewpoint, which is our 80M deduction, we are anyways fully covered.

Okay. Great. And my last one is just a clarification of something you just said earlier with regards to maturities at Vedanta Limited. Could you just repeat what you said? Do you -- did I hear correctly, you have about $1 billion at Vedanta Limited maturin g over the next couple of quarters?

That's correct. S o between Q3 and the Q4, the year second half, almost $1.2 billion are the maturities. And what I also say if you look at our cash flow plan for the second half, it will be more than $1.2 billion. And also our deep engagement with the capi tal markets, be it a PSU bankers, multinational bankers, FIIs, we feel, in fact, quite comfortable in terms of refinancing or repaying, both are the options.
Okay. So this is at a limited level, yes?
Great. Okay, thank you. That's all I had. Thank you very much.
So should one presume around $2 billion as bonds, around $0.5 billion for Oaktree and the balance is outstanding loans?

Public (C4) Ritesh Shah: Okay. That helps. Sir, I think you did clarify on the steel assets. I understand you are not giving any time lines over here. Just trying to have your thoughts. Has the company thought of securitizing the brand fee, given that's captive? And secondly, has the company even exercised advance pay and supply agreements for any of the commodities that we operate in?
Advance, I didn't get you the last one.

Sorry, advance pay and supply agreement. So this is a trade finance agreement. Typically, if you want to bolster your cash flows at this point in time... Arun M isra: So that's also a strategic initiative that we have launched on our marketing front, maybe with a few of the customers as and when we are able to secure such agreement with an advanced payment, not so much in steel. It happens mostly on our base metal side. We do have advanced payment agreement with long -term commitments with key international buyers, not so much to do with steel. But as and when it happens, we'll let you look.
Okay. But sir, my question is do we have anything of that sort right now on the balance sheet where we are already seeing the benefits? Arun M isra: No, I don't think on the steel side we have.

PRERNA HALWASIYA – DEPUTY HEAD, INVESTOR RELATIONS – VEDANTA LIMITED Vedanta Limited January 25, 202 4

Thank you, N eerav. Hello, everyone, and welcome to our third quarter of financial year '24 Earnings Conference Call. I'm Prerna Halwasiya. On behalf of the entire team of Vedanta, I would like to thank you for joining us today to discuss our financial results and busine ss performance. Today, from our leadership team, we have with us Mr. Arun Misra, our Executive Director; Mr. Ajay Goel, our Chief Financial Officer. Then, we additionally have Mr Akarsh Hebbar - Global Managing Director - Semiconductors and Display Businesses , Mr. Ajay Agarwal, President, Finance . Our business CEOs ; Mr. John Slaven - CEO , Aluminum business; Mr. Steve Moore - Deputy CEO, Oil & Gas. Along with him, we also have Mr. Vibhav Agarwal - CEO, Power Vertical; Mr. Chris Griffith - CEO of Base Metals Please note that today's entire discussion will be covered by the cautionary statement on Slide number 2 of the presentation. We will start with the update on our operational and financial performance, and then our leadership team will briefly speak about themselves and their vision for the individual businesses. And lastly, we'll open the floor for the Q&A . Now I would like to hand over the call to Mr. Arun Misra.

The business consumed highest -ever captive iron ore from its fully ramped up iron ore mines acquired last year. Quarterly saleable production stands at 341,000 tons, up 11% year -on-year with an EBITDA margin of $38 per ton. The business has a promising future of producing 2.4 million tons per annum with a cost of production of $546 per ton, deliveri ng an EBITDA of $301 million annually. Our Power plants cannot be forgotten when it comes to Business Delivery. Power Sector has delivered 9M EBITDA of around 90 Mn$ and has a huge potential to deliver 206 Mn$ annually with new power plants in line. FACOR recorded 53 KT as 9M production 10% up y -o-y with EBITDA margin of 140 $/T. Quarterly Ferrochrome production is 22KT up 15% y -o-y with EBITDA margin of 146 $/T. With an already approved capex of 2650 Cr, the business has outlook to produce 200 KT annually to deliver 100 Mn$ EBITDA.

rationale.rationale: The business being separated is SBI Funds Management Limited (SBIFM) — SBI Mutual Fund, the bank's asset-management joint venture with Amundi — which SBI is partially separating by listing it, not by demerging it; management repeatedly framed the purpose as "value unlocking" and, in Chairman C.S. Setty's words, "more importantly, value recognition for the industry" (Nov 2025), with SBI General Insurance named alongside AMC as the other listing candidate. The driver management gave was that SBI's own stock does not reflect the conglomerate's worth: Setty called SBI's valuation "a conundrum, considering our return on equity and growth metrics" (Nov 2025, with ROE 19.7%–20.68% and ROA >1% through FY26), and the same theme runs through the hidden-value argument on strategic holdings — of the group's ~7.3% NSE stake he said "the moment NSE gets listed, the whole shareholding by SBI will be available as reserve to us to mark to market" (May 2026). Explicitly NOT a capital-need story at first: in Nov 2025 Setty said "these two companies do not require capital at this juncture. Neither the parent requires because we just raised Rs. 25,000 crores" (the July 2025 QIP, India's largest, 4.5x oversubscribed on a >Rs. 1.1 trillion book, >60% cross-border), which is why timing was left to "respective boards"; by May 2026 the rationale had hardened into a capital one — the listing "will result in capital augmentation, CET-1" on top of CAR already up 115bps to 15.4%. The structure confirms it is monetisation, not a fix for the business: the IPO is a pure offer for sale (no fresh issue), SBI offering 6.3007% and JV partner Amundi India Holding 3.7006%, total up to 10.0013% / 203,709,239 shares at Rs. 1 face value, so no money reaches SBIFM itself. Management stressed that separation does not break the franchise link — SBIFM stays the country's largest AMC inside the "One SBI" cross-sell engine (a special dividend of ~Rs. 2,200 crore came up to the bank in Q3FY26, cross-sell/CVE income targeted at $1 billion, YONO "deep integration with subsidiary production"), and Setty was explicit that "Mutual fund, we are not fully exiting. So we still have potential to monetize further when market improves" (Feb 2026). The push came from the sell side and retail investors — Sushil Choksey (Indus Equity), Manoj Alimchandani and Kunal Shah (Citigroup) raised monetisation/value-unlocking on four of the five calls, Alimchandani even arguing in Feb 2026 that delaying the IPO five years could fetch three times the market cap — rather than from lenders or regulators; the only regulator-linked nudge cited was the SEBI chairman on NSE's listing. No problem with SBIFM's performance was ever offered as a reason: it was described only as "the largest AMC in the country," contributing Rs. 4,969.09 crore of FY26 total income, just 0.70% of group income.
rationale.evolution: May 2025 had no separation plan at all — only "we will continue to nurture these subsidiaries," while the bank instead took an enabling resolution for Rs. 25,000 crore of its own equity. By Aug 2025 Setty conceded "a couple of candidates for listing, but… there is no sense of urgency," and in Nov 2025 he named them — SBI AMC and SBI General — as the right candidates for "value unlocking" and "value recognition," with boards to set timing; the SBIFM stake-sale approval for 6.3007% followed on 6 Nov 2025 and the DRHP on 19 Mar 2026 (share count restated to 128,334,397 after a bonus issue and ESOP exercises). Feb 2026 added the retained-upside caveat ("we are not fully exiting") and May 2026 re-cast the deal as CET-1 capital augmentation to be completed within FY27. The plan then changed in execution in July 2026: a pre-IPO placement of 28,832,748 shares (1.4156%) to 30 investors at Rs. 574 for Rs. 1,655 crore on 9–10 July cut SBI's offer-for-sale from 6.3007% to 4.8851% (total offer 8.3933%), priced at Rs. 574 with allotment expected 18 July 2026.

points.point: No separation on the table: subsidiaries framed purely as value creators to be retained, while the bank instead took an enabling resolution to raise Rs. 25,000 crore of its own equity.
points.quote: Our subsidiaries are consistently performing well and continue to create significant value for all the stakeholders. We will continue to nurture these subsidiaries and maintain leadership position in the respective businesses.

points.point: First acknowledgement of listing candidates, asked for by Sushil Choksey (Indus Equity Advisors); Setty explicitly de-prioritised it because the Rs. 25,000 crore QIP had just closed.
points.quote: No, as we mentioned that we definitely have a couple of candidates for listing, but the timing is not very… there is no sense of urgency there, I believe.

points.point: The rationale stated in full for the first time, in answer to Choksey on the group's underperforming consolidated value: SBI AMC and SBI General named, with value unlocking and industry recognition of value as the purpose.
points.quote: But among these four major subsidiaries, we definitely would be looking at, as I mentioned several times, SBI AMC and SBI General are right candidates for listing in our stable. It also provides some value unlocking and, more importantly, value recognition for the industry.

points.point: Answering Kunal Shah (Citigroup) on what would trigger the decision, Setty ruled capital need out as a motive for either the subsidiaries or the parent, leaving timing and quantum to the subsidiary boards.
points.quote: I think we need to just look at, see, one is, as I mentioned earlier also, that these two companies do not require capital at this juncture.

points.point: The underlying grievance the separation is meant to address — SBI's own market valuation not tracking its ROE and growth — stated in the Chairman's opening remarks; Ashok Ajmera had quantified it as a Rs. 8.82 lakh crore market cap on Rs. 100 trillion of business versus Rs. 15.14 lakh crore for a Rs. 57 trillion peer.
points.quote: Although the current valuations of SBI are a conundrum, considering our return on equity and growth metrics, we are confident that they will eventually align with our fundamental and operational metrics, the institutionalized nature of our business and our market leadership in the coming years.

points.point: Retained-stake logic: asked by Manoj Alimchandani whether delaying the IPO five years could treble the market cap, Setty defended a partial sale that keeps future upside with SBI.
points.quote: Mutual fund, we are not fully exiting. So we still have potential to monetize further when market improves.

points.point: Why the AMC is worth separating while staying attached: it is already the country's largest AMC, upstreamed a Rs. 2,200 crore special dividend into SBI's Q3FY26 profit, and feeds a cross-sell income stream management targets at $1 billion.
points.quote: If I have to talk about one-off, I think the one item which is a special dividend we have received, around Rs. 2,200 crores from SBI Mutual Fund.

points.point: The rationale shifts to capital: with the AMC listing under way, Setty tied it to CET-1 augmentation supporting credit growth (the bank could already fund ~Rs. 12 trillion of growth, CAR 15.4%, up 115bps YoY).
points.quote: We are also seriously, as you are aware, we have embarked on listing SBI AMC and hopefully in this financial year we will be able to complete, which will result in capital augmentation, CET-1.

points.point: Same hidden-value argument applied to the group's ~7.3% NSE holding, which is not marked to market today — listing is the mechanism that converts unrecognised strategic stakes into reported reserves.
points.quote: But as you mentioned, I think the moment NSE gets listed, the whole shareholding by SBI will be available as reserve to us to mark to market.

points.point: 6 Nov 2025 board approval, restated in the 19 Mar 2026 DRHP filing: a pure offer for sale of up to 10.0013% (203,709,239 shares of Rs. 1 each) — SBI 6.3007% (128,334,397 shares) and JV partner Amundi India Holding 3.7006% (75,374,842 shares). No fresh issue, so no proceeds go to SBIFM.
points.quote: The IPO comprises an offer for sale of up to 128,334,397 Equity Shares (amounting to 6.3007% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFML) by State Bank of India, and of up to 75,374,842 Equity Shares (amounting to 3.7006% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFML) by Amundi India Holding.

points.point: Plan changed in execution: a pre-IPO secondary placement on 9–10 July 2026 moved 1.4156% of pre-offer capital to 30 investors at the eventual Rs. 574 offer price, raising Rs. 1,655 crore for SBI ahead of the book build.
points.quote: State Bank of India had entered into share purchase agreements each dated July 9, 2026 to sell, in aggregate, 2,88,32,748 equity shares of SBIFM of face value Rs. 1 (one) each ("Equity Shares"), being equivalent to 1.4156% of pre-Offer share capital of SBIFM, to a total of 30 (thirty) investors at Rs. 574.00 per Equity Share, for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 1,655.00 crores.

points.point: The 11 July 2026 addendum cut SBI's offer-for-sale by exactly the pre-IPO quantum, to 4.8851% (total offer 8.3933%); the offer was priced at Rs. 574 on 16 July with a Rs. 54 employee discount and allotment expected on or about 18 July 2026.
points.quote: The size of the offer for sale by the State Bank of India in the IPO has been revised from up to 128,334,397 Equity Shares (amounting to 6.3007% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFM) to up to 99,501,649 Equity Shares (amounting to 4.8851% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFM).

points.point: Materiality disclosed for the separated business: SBIFM's FY2026 total income of Rs. 4,969.09 crore is 0.70% of group income and its reserves 0.59% of group reserves — the separation is about price discovery, not size.
points.quote: Total income: Rs. 4,969.09 crores (0.70% of Total Income of SBI Group)

rationale.what_management_expects: For SBIFM: a listed market price that recognises India's largest AMC, with SBI retaining control, banca distribution and future monetisation upside. For SBI: value unlocking and "value recognition," CET-1 capital augmentation supporting 13-15% credit growth, hidden reserves surfaced (as with NSE), and valuation converging on >1% ROA and 15%+ through-cycle ROE. No margin or focus benefit was claimed.
rationale.gaps: No valuation target, expected proceeds, CET-1 basis points, or use of funds; no reason the offer was trimmed; Amundi's motive, SBI General's timeline, and post-listing distribution/royalty terms unexplained.

And: "An employee discount of Rs. 54.00 per Equity Share was offered to Eligible Employees in accordance with the terms and conditions stipulated in the RHP read with the Addendum." No new option/RSU/SAR plan in the listed entity, no exercise price or pricing date, and no management or insider shareholding is stated.

We have given our in-principal consent to them." No pledging disclosed.
